title: Acute exacerbation of COPD
blurb: Assess and manage an adult admitted with a COPD exacerbation: gases, controlled oxygen, nebulisers, steroids, NIV and ceilings of care.
question: Mrs Doherty, 67, is admitted with a COPD exacerbation. On a 28% Venturi mask her gas shows pH 7.29 and PCO2 8.4 kPa, and this persists despite nebulisers and steroids. What treatment is now indicated, and what must be agreed when it starts?

teach.body: Formally: an exacerbation is a sustained worsening of COPD symptoms from the person's stable state, beyond normal day-to-day variation, that is acute in onset (NG115). It is diagnosed clinically, not by a test. In plain English: they are more breathless, coughing more, and their sputum is often more or darker. In hospital the nurse's priorities are controlled oxygen, early blood gases, correctly driven nebulisers and watching for hypercapnic respiratory failure.

teach.caption: Other factors: coping at home, rapid onset, worsening oedema, significant comorbidity, chest X-ray changes, PaO2 below 7 kPa.

items: Arterial blood gases, recording the inspired oxygen concentration, then repeated according to response.
Chest X-ray and ECG (to exclude comorbidities).
Full blood count, urea and electrolytes; theophylline level if they take it.
Sputum for microscopy and culture if purulent; blood cultures if pyrexial.
Controlled oxygen to the individual target, usually 88–92%, while gases are awaited.

head: Treatment
Key point
rows: Nebuliser or hand-held; back to hand-held when stable
Driven by compressed air, O2 by nasal cannulae
Adjunct if poor response; check levels in 24 h
teach.caption: The driving gas for nebulised therapy should be specified on the prescription (NG115 1.3.12).

teach.h: Reading the gas: acute or chronic hypercapnia?
teach.body: A raised PCO2 (above 6 kPa) with a pH below 7.35 means acute respiratory acidosis: CO2 is building faster than the kidneys can compensate. A raised PCO2 with a normal pH (7.35 or above) and a high bicarbonate (above 28 mmol/L) suggests long-standing hypercapnia: keep 88–92% and repeat gases at 30–60 minutes to catch a rising PCO2 or falling pH.

steps.label: Controlled O2 88–92%
steps.sub: plus nebulisers, steroid, antibiotic if indicated

steps.label: Still acidotic?
steps.sub: pH below 7.35, PCO2 above 6 kPa after 30+ min

steps.label: Agree the plan
steps.sub: what if it fails; ceiling of treatment

teach.caption: NG115 1.3.30–1.3.32: NIV is the treatment of choice for persistent hypercapnic ventilatory failure despite optimal medical therapy. BTS 2017 section G gives the figures: NIV if pH stays below 7.35 with PCO2 above 6 kPa for more than 30 minutes after standard treatment.

teach.h: Worked scenario: Mrs Doherty on the respiratory unit
teach.body: Mrs Doherty's first gas showed pH 7.31 and PCO2 7.9 kPa. Staff nurse Joel kept her at 88–92% on a 28% Venturi mask, gave air-driven salbutamol with nasal oxygen and her first prednisolone 30 mg. Forty-five minutes later the gas shows pH 7.29, PCO2 8.4 kPa: persistent hypercapnic failure. The team starts NIV on the respiratory support unit and documents, with her, the plan if NIV fails, including whether intubation would be appropriate.

teach.text: Do not drive a nebuliser with oxygen at 6–8 L/min in a hypercapnic or acidotic COPD patient: use compressed air with nasal oxygen alongside. The opposite is true in acute asthma, where oxygen-driven nebulisers are preferred. And age or FEV1 alone must not decide whether someone is suitable for intubation.

items: ABG with FiO2 recorded for everyone admitted; CXR, ECG, FBC, U&E, cultures as indicated.
Controlled oxygen to the individual target; air-driven nebulisers if hypercapnic or acidotic.
Prednisolone 30 mg daily for 5 days, with clear instructions on stopping.
Persistent hypercapnic acidosis despite optimal treatment: NIV in a dedicated setting.
Agree a ceiling of treatment and a plan for deterioration when NIV starts.

summary: You can now prioritise the assessment of an adult admitted with a COPD exacerbation, give controlled oxygen and correctly driven nebulisers, and interpret a gas showing acute or chronic hypercapnia. You can also recognise when NIV is indicated and why a ceiling of treatment must be agreed.

A.q: What dose of oral prednisolone does NICE recommend for an acute exacerbation of COPD?
A.why: NG115 1.3.16 (2019): offer 30 mg oral prednisolone daily for 5 days.

whyNot.0: 40 mg for 7 days is not the NICE COPD regimen.
whyNot.2: 40–50 mg is the acute asthma dose, not COPD.
whyNot.3: 14 days is longer than NICE recommends.

A.q: Which investigation does NG115 recommend for everyone who arrives in hospital with a COPD exacerbation?
A.why: NG115 1.3.29: measure arterial blood gases and note the inspired oxygen concentration in everyone arriving at hospital with an exacerbation.

whyNot.0: Spirometry is not used during an acute exacerbation to guide treatment.
whyNot.1: CTPA is for suspected PE, not routine in exacerbations.
whyNot.3: PEF is used in asthma assessment, not as the core COPD admission test.

A.q: A patient with a COPD exacerbation has a raised PCO2 and pH 7.30. How should his salbutamol nebuliser be given?
A.why: NG115 1.3.11: if hypercapnic or acidotic, nebulisers should be driven by compressed air, with supplementary oxygen by nasal cannulae if needed.

whyNot.1: Oxygen-driven nebulisers risk worsening hypercapnia here.
whyNot.2: A reservoir mask is a high-concentration oxygen device, not a nebuliser.
whyNot.3: Oxygen as the driving gas is avoided in hypercapnic patients.

B.q: Which arterial blood gas pattern suggests long-standing (chronic) hypercapnia rather than acute respiratory acidosis?
B.why: BTS 2017: a raised PCO2 with pH 7.35 or above and a high bicarbonate (above 28 mmol/L) suggests long-standing hypercapnia.

whyNot.0: A low pH with raised PCO2 is acute respiratory acidosis.
whyNot.1: A low pH with low bicarbonate and normal PCO2 is metabolic acidosis.
whyNot.2: A low PCO2 with high pH is respiratory alkalosis.

B.q: A man with COPD is starting NIV for persistent hypercapnic respiratory failure. What must be documented at the start?
options: A target SpO2 of 94–98% while on NIV
A start date for pulmonary rehabilitation
A plan to stop his oral steroids that day
A deterioration plan and ceiling of care
B.why: NG115 1.3.32: when NIV starts there should be a clear plan covering what to do if the person deteriorates, and ceilings of therapy should be agreed.

whyNot.0: His target remains individualised, usually 88–92%, given hypercapnia.
whyNot.1: Rehabilitation is planned later and is not the start-of-NIV requirement.

B.q: A woman with COPD is on day 5 of prednisolone and is going home. What does NG115 emphasise for her discharge?
options: Continue prednisolone until her next clinic
Reduce the dose by 5 mg every week
Give clear instructions on stopping it
Stop her inhalers while on steroids
B.why: NG115 1.3.20: give people, particularly those discharged from hospital, clear instructions on why, when and how to stop their corticosteroid treatment.

whyNot.0: The course is 5 days, not open-ended.
whyNot.1: A slow weekly taper is not the NICE regimen for a 5-day course.
whyNot.3: Inhaled therapy continues alongside oral steroids.

C.q: Mr Shah, 75, with COPD, has pH 7.31 and PCO2 7.6 kPa on arrival. After 45 minutes of controlled oxygen, nebulisers and steroids, a repeat gas shows pH 7.30 and PCO2 7.9 kPa. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Increase to a reservoir mask at 15 L/min
Give IV theophylline and recheck tomorrow
Start NIV in a dedicated setting
C.why: Persistent hypercapnic acidosis despite optimal medical therapy: NIV is the treatment of choice (NG115 1.3.30), delivered in a dedicated setting by trained staff (1.3.31). BTS 2017 section G: start NIV if respiratory acidosis persists for more than 30 minutes after standard treatment.

whyNot.1: Theophylline is an adjunct and does not replace NIV for persistent acidosis.
whyNot.3: Changing the oxygen device does not treat ventilatory failure.

C.q: A registrar says a man with an exacerbation is 'too old at 82 for intubation' and wants that in the notes. What does NICE say about this decision?
options: His family should make the decision
C.why: NG115 1.3.34: consider functional status, BMI, oxygen need when stable, comorbidities and previous ICU admissions, as well as age and FEV1. Neither age nor FEV1 should be used in isolation.

whyNot.0: Age by itself must not decide suitability.
whyNot.1: FEV1 by itself must not decide suitability.
whyNot.3: Families inform the decision, but the clinical assessment and the patient's wishes guide it.

C.q: Mrs Ahmed, 70, with COPD, has an SpO2 of 86% on a 24% Venturi mask, a respiratory rate of 26 and a normal pH. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Remove oxygen and repeat the gas on air
Change to 28% Venturi and recheck gas
Give a reservoir mask at 15 L/min
Start NIV straight away on the ward
C.why: She is below her 88–92% target with a normal pH. Increase controlled oxygen (e.g. 28% Venturi) to reach target and repeat gases after 30–60 minutes (BTS 2017).

whyNot.0: Removing oxygen would worsen her hypoxaemia.
whyNot.3: NIV is for persistent hypercapnic acidosis; her pH is normal.

reteach.title: Two problems in one patient
reteach.question: In a COPD exacerbation, why does the nurse watch both the oxygen and the carbon dioxide?

blocks.body: An exacerbation can cause two problems: not enough oxygen getting in (hypoxaemia) and not enough carbon dioxide getting out (hypercapnia). Oxygen fixes the first but, given too freely, can worsen the second. So oxygen is controlled to 88–92%, and the gas tells you about CO2 and pH. If CO2 keeps rising with a falling pH despite treatment, the patient needs help to breathe: NIV.

blocks.text: A normal SpO2 tells you nothing about CO2. Only the blood gas shows hypercapnia and acidosis.

explain.body: Everyone admitted: ABG with FiO2 noted, chest X-ray, ECG, FBC and U&E. Sputum culture if purulent; blood cultures if pyrexial; theophylline level if taking it.

test.q: When does NG115 advise sending blood cultures in a patient admitted with a COPD exacerbation?
options: If the patient has a fever
If they already use home LTOT
test.why: NG115 1.3.3: take blood cultures if the person has pyrexia.

whyNot.0: Purulent sputum triggers a sputum sample, not blood cultures.
whyNot.2: NG115 does not set a CRP trigger for blood cultures.
whyNot.3: LTOT is a factor favouring hospital care, not a culture trigger.

explain.body: Controlled oxygen to the individual target. If hypercapnic or acidotic, nebulisers are driven by compressed air with oxygen by nasal cannulae. Prescriptions state the driving gas. Switch to hand-held inhalers once stable.

test.q: Why does NG115 advise changing patients back to hand-held inhalers as soon as they are stable?
options: It reduces the steroid dose needed
test.why: NG115 1.3.10: change to hand-held inhalers as soon as the condition has stabilised, because this may allow earlier discharge.

whyNot.1: Pneumonia risk is not the reason given.
whyNot.2: Inhaler device does not change the steroid course.
whyNot.3: Speed of action is not the reason NICE gives.

explain.body: Oral corticosteroids for everyone admitted unless contraindicated: prednisolone 30 mg daily for 5 days. Consider osteoporosis prophylaxis with frequent courses; explain how and when to stop.

test.q: A man with COPD has had several prednisolone courses this year. What does NG115 advise the team to think about?
test.why: NG115 1.3.18: think about osteoporosis prophylaxis for people who need frequent courses of oral corticosteroids.

whyNot.1: Anticoagulation is not linked to steroid courses.
whyNot.2: Routine potassium supplements are not recommended for this.
whyNot.3: Annual CT is not an NG115 response to steroid use.

explain.body: NIV is the treatment of choice for persistent hypercapnic ventilatory failure despite optimal medical therapy, in a dedicated setting with trained staff, with a deterioration plan and agreed ceiling of treatment.

test.q: Where does NICE recommend NIV is delivered for COPD exacerbations?
options: Any ward with a free side room
A general ward overnight then review
A dedicated unit with trained staff
test.why: NG115 1.3.31: NIV should be delivered in a dedicated setting with staff trained and experienced in its use and aware of its limitations.

whyNot.0: A side room without trained staff does not meet the standard.
whyNot.1: A corridor lacks the setting and staffing required.
whyNot.2: A general ward without NIV-trained staff does not meet the standard.
